properties.natural_language: LOG opcodes must never execute in a static call context; any LOG0-LOG4 instruction dispatched during STATICCALL must raise WriteInStaticContext before any state modification occurs.
Before LOG execution proceeds, the static context flag must be verified as false; only non-static execution contexts permit LOG operations.
When memory_start_index + size overflows uint256, the memory expansion gas calculation must treat the required size as exceeding available gas, causing an out-of-gas exception.
Topics for LOG opcodes must be popped from the stack in order: memory_start_index first, then size, then topic values sequentially from stack positions.
Memory read operations for LOG data must automatically expand memory when reading beyond current bounds, with gas charged for the expansion.
LOG operations must be atomic: either the complete log entry (address, topics, data) is appended to the logs list, or the operation reverts entirely with no partial log recorded.
The contract address recorded in every log entry must be the address of the currently executing contract, preventing log spoofing across contracts.
After popping all LOG parameters from the stack, exactly (2 + num_topics) values have been consumed: memory_start_index, size, and 0-4 topic values.
After topic conversion, each topic value must be exactly 32 bytes in big-endian format.
After LOG instruction completes, the program counter must be incremented by exactly 1.
After successful gas charging for LOG, the total gas deducted equals GAS_LOG + GAS_LOG_DATA * size + GAS_LOG_TOPIC * num_topics + memory_expansion_cost.
If any gas charge step fails due to insufficient gas, the LOG operation must transition to out-of-gas state and no log entry is recorded.
After creating a Meta EIP draft, it must contain a codename, activation block placeholder, timeline fields, and a list of included EIPs.
After freezing hard fork changes, no additional EIPs may be added to the Meta EIP; the specification is locked.
After hard fork activation on the network, the Meta EIP status must be Final and immutable; no further modifications are permitted.
After client implementation verification succeeds, at least 3 major execution clients must have working implementations of the EIP.
After security check identifies issues, the EIP must be rejected from the current hard fork and cannot proceed to acceptance.
For an EIP to pass implementation checks, at least 3 of the main execution clients (Geth, Nethermind, Besu, Erigon) representing >80% of network participation must have working implementations.
Emergency security patches may bypass the standard timeline through expedited All Core Devs decision, but must still undergo basic review.
If the soft implementation deadline is missed, the EIP may be excluded from the hard fork unless an explicit exception is granted by All Core Devs.
All Core Devs governance decisions must represent good-faith consensus of the developer community and not be captured by any single interest.
Client teams must have sufficient resources to implement approved EIPs within the specified timeline to avoid rushed implementations or security vulnerabilities.
The majority of the network (validators and users) must upgrade their clients before the activation block to prevent chain splits.
After setting the acceptance deadline, no new EIP proposals may be submitted for inclusion after that date.
After setting the mainnet activation block, all clients must include the upgrade at exactly that block number.
All eth_getProof requests from external RPC clients must be validated for correct parameter format (address, storage keys array, block identifier) before processing.
The number of storage keys in an eth_getProof request must be bounded by implementation-defined limits to prevent denial of service.
Proof data received from an untrusted RPC provider must not be trusted until cryptographically verified against a trusted stateRoot.
The trusted block header used for proof verification must be obtained from a reliable consensus source (beacon chain or light client), not from the same untrusted RPC provider.
Cryptographic proof verification must use keccak256 hash comparisons without trusting any intermediate data from the RPC provider.
When a requested block has been pruned, the RPC endpoint must return an error rather than incomplete or incorrect proof data.
Non-existence proofs must include all Merkle-Patricia trie nodes down to the point where the path diverges or branch is empty.
The verifier must have access to a trusted block header from a reliable source before attempting any proof verification.
It must be computationally infeasible for an attacker to forge Merkle proofs that validate against a correct stateRoot.
The RPC endpoint must have access to the full state trie for the requested block to generate complete proofs.
After proof assembly, the accountProof array must contain RLP-serialized nodes forming a valid path from stateRoot to the target account.
After account data retrieval, the response must include nonce, balance, codeHash, and storageHash fields.
After successful verification, the verified account and storage data is cryptographically authenticated against the trusted stateRoot.
Any contract or EOA may invoke the RIPEMD-160 precompile with arbitrary input data; the precompile must handle all inputs safely without crashing.
Untrusted external data provided for hashing must be accepted without restriction on content, as hash functions are designed for arbitrary input.
Before hash computation, sufficient gas must be available; gas cost is GAS_RIPEMD160 + GAS_RIPEMD160_WORD * ceil32(input_length)/32.
When input data length is zero, the precompile must produce the RIPEMD-160 hash of empty input, left-padded to 32 bytes.
The gas constants GAS_RIPEMD160 (600) and GAS_RIPEMD160_WORD (120) must be used for gas calculation.
The 20-byte RIPEMD-160 hash output must be left-padded with 12 zero bytes to produce a 32-byte output (hash at bytes 12-31).
The hashlib RIPEMD-160 implementation must produce cryptographically correct, standards-compliant output for all inputs.
Finding collisions in RIPEMD-160 must remain computationally infeasible for practical attack scenarios.
After RIPEMD-160 computation, the output is a deterministic 20-byte hash: same input always produces same output.
After setting EVM output, the evm.output field contains exactly 32 bytes (12 zero bytes + 20 byte hash).
After RLP decoding the block header, all Prague-specific fields including requests_hash, blob_gas_used, and excess_blob_gas must be present.
After all header validations pass, the block header is considered valid and the block can be processed.
After any single header validation fails, the entire block must be rejected as invalid.
After crediting a withdrawal recipient, the account balance must increase by exactly the withdrawal amount in Gwei.
After computing the withdrawals trie root, it must match the withdrawals_root in the block header.
After detecting the transaction type, the receipt must be encoded with the correct type prefix byte (none for legacy, 0x01-0x04 for typed transactions).
After computing the requests hash, it must be a SHA2-256 hash (not Keccak) of the serialized protocol requests.
The request types contributing to requests_hash must be defined by EIP-7685 (validator deposits, withdrawals, consolidations).
The ommers field must be present as an empty tuple in PoS blocks, and ommers_hash must equal the hash of the empty list.
The parent_beacon_block_root must match the beacon block corresponding to this execution block, as provided by the consensus layer.
Beacon chain withdrawal data must be authentic and unforgeable; forged withdrawals would allow arbitrary balance inflation.
The Engine API between execution and consensus layers must be correctly implemented to prevent consensus splits.
An attacker must not be able to manipulate block timestamps or numbers to bypass validation rules.
All nodes must upgrade to support EIP-7702 SetCodeTransaction (type 4) before Prague activation to prevent chain splits.
Withdrawal indices must be sequential and unique within a block; no duplicate or out-of-order indices are permitted.
After the Dencun fork transition is applied, the network must operate under Deneb/Cancun consensus rules with all component EIPs active.
After EL activation, EIP-1153 (TLOAD/TSTORE), EIP-4844 (blob tx), EIP-5656 (MCOPY), EIP-6780 (SELFDESTRUCT restriction), and EIP-7516 (BLOBBASEFEE) must all be simultaneously active.
After CL activation, EIP-4788 (beacon root), EIP-7044 (exit validity), EIP-7045 (attestation slots), and EIP-7514 (churn limit) must all be active.
All execution layer EIP changes must be applied atomically at the fork block boundary with no ordering dependencies between individual EIPs.
Activation epochs must be chosen such that the first slot of the activation epoch corresponds to the expected execution layer fork timestamp.
All client implementations must have updated to support Dencun before the activation epoch to prevent network partitioning.
Testnet activations on Goerli, Sepolia, and Holesky must serve as sufficient validation before mainnet activation.
All individual EIPs included in the Dencun meta EIP must have been thoroughly reviewed for security vulnerabilities.
The mainnet activation epoch for Dencun must be 269568 (timestamp 1710338135); this value is immutable once set.
All eth_chainId requests from external RPC clients must be parsed and validated before processing; no authentication is required for this read-only method.
When a wallet initiates transaction signing, the chain ID must be queried from the connected node to ensure correct replay protection.
If the chain ID obtained from the node does not match the expected network, the wallet must detect the mismatch and warn the user before signing.
Chain ID must remain constant during normal operation and only change during hard forks that explicitly modify the chain ID.
Chain ID must be encoded as a 0x-prefixed hexadecimal string with no leading zeros (except '0x0' for value 0).
The node must return the correct chain ID; a compromised or misconfigured node returning wrong chain ID could cause replay attacks.
Clients must prefer eth_chainId over net_version for chain identification, as network ID and chain ID may differ.
Wallet applications must verify chain ID before signing every transaction; stale cached values could lead to wrong-chain signing.
After including chain ID in the transaction signature per EIP-155, the signed transaction is replay-protected across different chains.
When the head block does not specify a chain ID (pre-EIP-155), the method must return an error indicating unavailability.
After calculating the maximum refund, the cap must be gas_used divided by 5 (20% of gas used), not the previous 50%.
After applying the refund cap, the actual refund must equal min(accumulated_refund_counter, gas_used / 5).
After crediting refund to sender, the effective gas used is reduced by the refund amount.
When storage transitions from nonzero to zero (clearing), the refund counter must increase by exactly 4800 gas.
When a slot transitions zero to nonzero to zero within the same transaction, the refund counter must increase by exactly 19900 gas.
When a storage value is reverted to its original value, the refund counter must increase by exactly 4900 gas.
After SELFDESTRUCT execution, NO gas refund must be added to the refund counter (EIP-3529 removes SELFDESTRUCT refund).
The 19900 gas refund applies when: original_value == 0 AND current_value != 0 AND new_value == 0 (slot empty, set, then cleared in same tx).
The 20% refund cap must be sufficient to prevent gas token exploitation while preserving legitimate storage clearing incentives.
Block producers must not be significantly impacted by the reduced maximum effective gas capacity (1.25x vs previous 2x block gas limit).
EIP-2929/2930 access list costs used in SSTORE_CLEARS_SCHEDULE calculation must be correctly integrated.
With the 20% max refund cap, the maximum effective gas usage in a block is bounded at 125% of the block gas limit.
All silent signing permission requests from external applications must pass through user consent UI before granting any permission.
Application permission requests must include chain ID, contract address, function signatures, and expiry timestamp; all fields must be validated before prompting user.
When a dApp submits a transaction for silent signing, the permission secret must be verified and the transaction must be within the permitted scope before signing.
The wallet consent UI must display the full permission scope (contract, functions, duration) to ensure informed user consent.
The permissionSecret must be generated using a cryptographically secure random number generator with at least 128 bits of entropy.
Permission scope restrictions must apply to 4-byte function selectors; overloaded functions with the same name but different parameters are distinguished by their selectors.
If a permission secret is suspected compromised, the user must be able to immediately revoke the permission.
Users must understand the permission scope being granted and make informed consent decisions.
An attacker must not be able to intercept or steal the permissionSecret from the application; if stolen, they could submit transactions within granted scope until expiry.
The wallet implementation must correctly enforce scope restrictions on every silent-signed transaction without exception.
WalletConnect bridge servers used for mobile must not tamper with or leak transaction data or permission secrets.
After user grants permission, a cryptographically random permissionSecret token must be generated and returned to the application.
After permission expiry check finds timestamp exceeded, the permission must transition to expired state and reject all further signing requests.
After secret verification fails, the transaction must be rejected and no signing occurs.
After scope check finds transaction targets unpermitted contract or function, the transaction must be rejected.
After successful silent signing and broadcast, the signed transaction has been submitted to the blockchain network.
After all validation checks pass (chain ID, contract, functions, timestamp), the permission request is ready for user consent.
Both temporal and scope boundaries must be enforced simultaneously on every silent signing request; neither can be bypassed independently.
All signing requests from validator clients must be authenticated before the signing key is accessed.
BLS private keys must be stored in HSM or secrets manager at rest; loading into memory must only occur during signing operations.
HTTP requests arriving over untrusted networks must pass authentication and rate limiting before reaching the signing logic.
All HTTP client requests must be validated for correct HTTP method, content type, JSON syntax, and required fields before processing.
Communication between validator client and signer must use TLS/HTTPS to prevent eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks.
If TLS is not used, the communication is subject to eavesdropping risk exposing signatures to interception.
The 'data' field in signing requests must be treated as raw bytes encoded as a hexadecimal string.
The 'fork' parameter must follow the Ethereum 2.0 fork structure with epoch and version fields.
Signing operations must complete within reasonable HTTP timeout bounds; clients must implement their own timeouts.
Slashing protection validation modules must check for duplicate attestations and conflicting block proposals at minimum.
The validator client requesting signatures must be trusted and authorized to sign for the requested key identifier.
The network between validator client and signer must be secured with TLS and not subject to man-in-the-middle attacks.
Operators must implement slashing protection external to this API to prevent signing duplicate or conflicting messages.
Physical access to the signer node must be restricted to prevent memory dump attacks that could extract private keys.
The HSM or secrets manager storing private keys must be properly configured and secure; compromise leads to total key security loss.
After successful BLS signature computation, the response must be HTTP 200 with a JSON body containing the signature as a hex string.
After request parsing fails, the response must be HTTP 400 Bad Request.
After key lookup fails for the requested identifier, the response must be HTTP 404 Not Found.
After signing completes, private key material must be zeroized from memory to prevent residual key extraction.
After authentication fails, the request must be rejected and no key access or signing occurs.
After rate limit is exceeded, the request must be rejected to prevent denial-of-service attacks.
After BLS domain validation fails, the response must be HTTP 400 Bad Request indicating unrecognized domain.
The BLS domain for signing must be restricted to exactly: beacon_proposer, beacon_attester, or randao; no other domains are allowed.
All errors must be logged for operational monitoring regardless of whether they are client errors (4xx) or server errors (5xx).
After all validation checks pass (HTTP method, content type, JSON, required fields, BLS domain, hash format), the request is fully validated for signing.
